newsitem.title: KENYA: FEATURE - Political climate tense as Kenya prepares for polls.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Political climate tense as Kenya prepares for polls.

text.p: Kenya's divided opposition is girding up for a pre-election offensive to win constitutional reforms, but the signs are that President Daniel arap Moi is ready to suppress protests with force.

Worried Kenyans and foreigners fear trouble is brewing in the run-up to the polls. The capital, Nairobi, got a taste of what may be in store when security forces dispersed a banned opposition rally on May 31. Two days of rioting followed.
Five years after the East African country's first multi-party polls, themselves marred by violence and alleged rigging, the political debate is tense and laced with the language of violence.
"In 1992, the violence was in the Rift Valley but in 1997 it will also be in the urban areas, expecially Nairobi," columnist John Githongo wrote in the East African, a respected weekly.
Moi must call the presidential and parliamentary polls by the end of the year. Now aged 73, Moi took office in 1978 and is seeking what the current constitution says must be his final five-year term.

In 1992 Moi won with less than 35 percent of the vote, exploiting the opposition's failure to field a single candidate. Five years later, the same scenario is unfolding with almost the same opposition leaders still unable to unite against Moi or his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU).
APATHY TAKES ROOT AS REFORMS BLOCKED
The difference is that apathy has taken root and popular anger about corruption, poverty and injustice is seldom channelled through established political parties.

By June 8 only 3.8 million Kenyans had registered to vote, according to the National Electoral Commission. With the June 22 registration deadline approaching, this is a little more than a third of the estimated electorate of 10 million.
Opposition parties are bedevilled by personal and tribal rivalries.

Moi is from the Kalenjin group of small tribes and his powerbase is not within the most populous ethnic groups, the Kikuyu, Luo and Luhya. But the opposition has failed to unite the Big Three ethnic groups, each of which has its own political champions.

The opposition is trying to overcome the handicap by presenting a united facade in their campaign for the repeal or review of constitutional provisions which give the presidency almost total power or which restrict basic freedoms.

"If the government refuses to implement these reforms and stage-manages another election then the political message will be that power will never change by peaceful means," opposition politician Paul Muite told Reuters.
"The situation is ripe for individuals who believe that only armed conflict can bring change," he said.
A loose coalition of opposition parties, church leaders and pressure groups has called for a protest in Nairobi outside parliament on June 19, to coincide with the annual budget debate.
Opposition leaders Raila Odinga and Kenneth Matiba have announced nine rallies across Kenya on June 21 to press for minimum constitutional reforms before the elections.
MOI READY TO USE FORCE AGAINST "FREE-FOR-ALL"
The government has banned them and Moi appears ready to prove he is not rattled by the sudden challenge to his rule.
"I warn opposition politicians they should not move around thinking Kenya is just a free-for-all," he said on June 4.
"From now henceforth law and order will be maintained by the government," he added.
The Sunday Nation reported at the weekend that anti-riot police were already staging a show of force in the western city of Kisumu, Odinga's fief, a week before the planned rally there.
Moi's only minor concession, to replace the Public Order Act with one called Peaceful Assemblies, was swiftly dismissed by opposition leaders after it was tabled in parliament last week.
The new legislation would still require political parties to obtain approval before holding meetings. Such permits from the all-powerful provincial administrations are seldom given.
The proposed Bill "shows clearly that democratic space is still being denied to the opposition and civil society," James Orengo, a leader of the FORD Kenya party, told reporters.
OPPOSITION GETS MORAL SUPPORT ABROAD
Kenya's opposition can rely on stout moral support from any number of foreign human rights organisations whose reports portray Moi's government as one of the most autocratic in Africa.
Amnesty International was the latest to condemn human rights abuses and repressive laws.

"We believe that the violence that results from the application of these unjust laws will not allow the election to take place in a climate that is conducive to producing a legitimate government for tomorrow," the London-based group's secretary-general, Pierre Sane, said in Nairobi on June 11.
A day later, the government shot back with a statement accusing Amnesty of inciting Kenyans against the government.
Despite progress on economic reforms, Moi is constantly under pressure from Western donors and embassies in Nairobi on political issues.
Diplomats say the United States is leading the pressure, as it did before the 1992 polls, and Washington increasingly perceives Moi as an ageing autocrat who must accept change before it is too late.
But European Union (EU) policy on Kenya is less forthright, blunted partly by Britain, the former colonial power and biggest foreign investor.
British officials frequently caution that opposition leaders are hardly model democrats and most are stained by past membership of the ruling KANU elite.
